title: What are the main caching patterns and when do you use each — Cache-Aside (app checks cache, on miss loads DB then populates cache), Read-Through / Write-Through / Write-Behind — and how does an architecture evolve from in-memory (Caffeine) to a distributed cache (Redis) once there are multiple app instances?
shortTitle: What are the main caching patterns and when do you use each?

s1_definition.profdef: The main caching patterns differ in who talks to the database and when. In Cache-Aside (also called lazy loading), the application code owns the logic: on a read it checks the cache first, and on a miss it loads from the database, populates the cache, and returns the value. In Read-Through, the cache itself owns loading: the application only asks the cache, and the cache transparently fetches from the database on a miss through a configured loader. In Write-Through, every write goes through the cache, which synchronously writes to both the cache and the database before returning, keeping them consistent at the cost of write latency. In Write-Behind (write-back), the write updates the cache immediately and the database is updated asynchronously a short time later, giving fast writes but risking data loss if the cache fails before flushing. The architecture evolves from an in-memory cache like Caffeine, which lives inside a single application process, to a distributed cache like Redis once you run multiple application instances, because a per-process cache is not shared, so instances would hold inconsistent copies and a write on one instance would not invalidate the stale copy on another.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, imagine the balance ledgers are in the basement vault (the database), and the teller keeps a notepad of recently-looked-up balances on the desk (the cache). Cache-Aside is the teller's own habit: "let me check my notepad; not there? I'll run to the vault, note it down, and tell you." Read-Through is like having an assistant who you always ask, and the assistant quietly runs to the vault for you when the notepad is empty. Write-Through is the careful teller who, whenever a balance changes, updates both the notepad and the vault ledger at the same time before serving the next customer — always consistent, but a touch slower. Write-Behind is the fast teller who scribbles the change on the notepad instantly and promises to walk it down to the vault in a few minutes — quick, but if he spills coffee on the notepad before the vault trip, the change is lost. And when the bank grows from one teller to ten, each with a separate notepad, the notepads disagree, so the bank installs one shared whiteboard everyone reads and writes (Redis) instead of private notepads (Caffeine).
s1_definition.oneliner: Cache-Aside puts the load-on-miss logic in the application, Read-Through delegates it to the cache, Write-Through writes to cache and database synchronously for consistency, Write-Behind writes to cache first and the database asynchronously for speed, and you move from a per-process cache like Caffeine to a shared distributed cache like Redis the moment multiple instances must agree.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The main caching patterns differ in who talks to the database and when. In Cache-Aside (also called lazy loading), the application code owns the logic: on a read it checks the cache first, and on a miss it loads from the database, populates the cache, and returns the value. In Read-Through, the cache itself owns loading: the application only asks the cache, and the cache transparently fetches from the database on a miss through a configured loader. In Write-Through, every write goes through the cache, which synchronously writes to both the cache and the database before returning, keeping them consistent at the cost of write latency. In Write-Behind (write-back), the write updates the cache immediately and the database is updated asynchronously a short time later, giving fast writes but risking data loss if the cache fails before flushing. The architecture evolves from an in-memory cache like Caffeine, which lives inside a single application process, to a distributed cache like Redis once you run multiple application instances, because a per-process cache is not shared, so instances would hold inconsistent copies and a write on one instance would not invalidate the stale copy on another.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, imagine the balance ledgers are in the basement vault (the database), and the teller keeps a notepad of recently-looked-up balances on the desk (the cache). Cache-Aside is the teller's own habit: "let me check my notepad; not there? I'll run to the vault, note it down, and tell you." Read-Through is like having an assistant who you always ask, and the assistant quietly runs to the vault for you when the notepad is empty. Write-Through is the careful teller who, whenever a balance changes, updates both the notepad and the vault ledger at the same time before serving the next customer — always consistent, but a touch slower. Write-Behind is the fast teller who scribbles the change on the notepad instantly and promises to walk it down to the vault in a few minutes — quick, but if he spills coffee on the notepad before the vault trip, the change is lost. And when the bank grows from one teller to ten, each with a separate notepad, the notepads disagree, so the bank installs one shared whiteboard everyone reads and writes (Redis) instead of private notepads (Caffeine).

**One line to remember:** Cache-Aside puts the load-on-miss logic in the application, Read-Through delegates it to the cache, Write-Through writes to cache and database synchronously for consistency, Write-Behind writes to cache first and the database asynchronously for speed, and you move from a per-process cache like Caffeine to a shared distributed cache like Redis the moment multiple instances must agree.

sections.s2_technical:
Cache-Aside is the most common pattern and the default for most services. The application controls everything: on a read, it first does a cache get; if the value is present (a hit) it returns it, and if it is absent (a miss) it reads from the database, writes the value into the cache with a time-to-live, and returns it. The appeal is that the application is in full control and the cache only ever holds data that was actually requested, so it is naturally resilient — if the cache is down, the application falls back to the database and still works. The trade-offs are that the first read of any key is always a miss (a cold start), and you must handle invalidation on writes yourself, typically by deleting or updating the cache entry when the underlying data changes. For example reading a balance: `var cached = cache.get(id); if (cached == null) { cached = db.load(id); cache.put(id, cached, ttl); }`.

Read-Through moves the load-on-miss responsibility into the cache itself. The application only ever asks the cache, and the cache is configured with a loader function that it invokes on a miss to fetch from the database, store the result, and return it. This makes the application code simpler (no explicit database fallback on reads) and centralizes the loading logic, which is convenient when many call sites read the same data. The cost is tighter coupling to a cache that supports this mode, and the same cold-start behavior. Caffeine's LoadingCache is a Read-Through cache: you build it with a loader, and `cache.get(id)` returns the cached value or transparently calls the loader on a miss.

Write-Through and Write-Behind are about the write path. In Write-Through, a write is sent to the cache, which synchronously writes to the database and updates its own copy before the call returns, so the cache and the database are always consistent and a subsequent read is guaranteed to hit a fresh value. The price is that every write pays the database write latency plus the cache write, so writes are slower, and you may cache data that is never read again. Write-Through pairs naturally with Read-Through so that the cache is always the single interface for both reads and writes. In Write-Behind, the write updates the cache immediately and returns, and a background process flushes the change to the database after a delay, often batching many writes together. This gives very fast, high-throughput writes and can coalesce repeated updates to the same key into one database write, but it introduces a durability risk: if the cache node fails before the flush, those writes are lost, and it introduces a window where the database is behind the cache. Write-Behind suits high-write workloads that tolerate eventual durability, such as counters, metrics, or view counts, and is dangerous for money movement where every write must be durable.

Choosing among them is driven by the read-write mix and the consistency and durability needs. For read-heavy data where occasional staleness is acceptable, Cache-Aside with a short time-to-live is the simplest and most robust choice, which is why it dominates. When you want to hide the loading logic and centralize it, Read-Through is cleaner. When reads must always see the latest write and you can afford slower writes, Write-Through gives that consistency. When writes are frequent and you prioritize throughput over immediate durability, Write-Behind is the tool, used carefully. Many real systems combine them: Cache-Aside for reads with explicit invalidation on writes is extremely common, while Write-Through plus Read-Through is common when the cache is treated as the system of engagement in front of the database.

The evolution from Caffeine to Redis is driven by moving from one application instance to many. Caffeine is an in-process, in-memory cache: it is extremely fast because a lookup is just a method call against a concurrent map in the same JVM, with no network hop, and it is perfect for a single instance or for data that is identical and safe to duplicate per instance (like reference data). But the moment you run multiple instances behind a load balancer, each instance has its own private Caffeine cache, so they are not shared and they drift apart: a write that updates or invalidates one instance's cache leaves the other instances serving stale data, because they never heard about the change. This inconsistency is unacceptable for data like balances. The fix is a distributed cache like Redis, which lives outside the application processes so all instances read and write the same shared cache, and an invalidation from any instance is immediately visible to all. The cost is that every cache access is now a network call (hundreds of microseconds instead of nanoseconds) and Redis is an additional system to operate and scale.

A senior nuance is that you do not have to choose one — a very common high-performance pattern is multi-level caching, where a small, short-lived Caffeine L1 cache in each instance sits in front of a shared Redis L2 cache, so the hottest keys are served at nanosecond speed from L1 while L2 keeps instances roughly consistent and absorbs the misses. The trade-off there is the short L1 time-to-live, which bounds how stale an L1 entry can be. Another nuance is invalidation strategy: with a distributed cache you can either delete the key on write (and let the next read repopulate via Cache-Aside) or update it (Write-Through), and deletion is usually safer because it avoids caching a value that may be wrong due to a concurrent write. A final nuance is that caching introduces consistency trade-offs that you must name explicitly — a cache with a time-to-live is eventually consistent by definition, and whether that is acceptable depends on the data, so you cache a displayed balance with a short time-to-live but you never cache the authoritative balance used to authorize a debit.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India's account service caches balances, and the team works through the patterns as the system grows.

Problem 1 — Reading balances hit the database on every request and was slow under load. The team added Cache-Aside: check the cache, on a miss load the database and populate the cache. This is the Cache-Aside read pattern.

Problem 2 — The load-on-miss logic was duplicated across many call sites, so the team switched reads to Read-Through via a loading cache that fetches on a miss, and made writes Write-Through so a balance update writes cache and database together and reads always see the latest. This is Read-Through and Write-Through.

Problem 3 — The service scaled to multiple instances, and each instance's in-process Caffeine cache drifted: a write on one instance left others serving a stale balance. The team moved the shared balances to Redis so all instances read and write the same cache. This is the Caffeine-to-Redis evolution.

We will model a cache abstraction with Cache-Aside, Read-Through, Write-Through, and Write-Behind variants over an account store, then show two instances with private in-process caches drifting, and the same two instances sharing one distributed cache staying consistent.

The code will have an `AccountStore` (the database), a `Cache` interface, a `LocalCache` (Caffeine-style per-process) and a `DistributedCache` (Redis-style shared), an `AccountService` demonstrating each pattern, and a demo showing drift versus consistency.

```bash

java CachingPatternsDemo

# Choosing a pattern:
#   Cache-Aside   : read-heavy, tolerate short staleness, app controls load+invalidation (default)
#   Read-Through  : centralize load-on-miss in the cache (Caffeine LoadingCache)
#   Write-Through : reads must see latest write; accept slower writes (consistency)
#   Write-Behind  : high write throughput, tolerate eventual durability (counters/metrics)
# Caffeine → Redis: single instance = Caffeine (nanosecond, in-process);
#   multiple instances = Redis (shared, consistent) — private caches DRIFT on writes.
# Often BOTH: short-TTL Caffeine L1 in front of shared Redis L2.
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two accounts in the database, read and written through the various patterns, first on one instance and then across two instances.

Step 1 — The first Cache-Aside read of Rajesh's balance misses the cache, so the service loads it from the database, stores it in the cache, and returns it. The second read hits the cache and returns instantly without touching the database. The application owned the load-on-miss logic.

Step 2 — A Write-Through update sets Rajesh's balance to a new value by writing both the database and the cache in the same call, so the immediately following read sees the new value from the cache with no staleness. The cache and database stayed consistent because the write updated both.

Step 3 — Two instances are created, each with its own private in-process cache. Both read Priya's balance and cache the same value. Then instance one performs a write-through that updates the database and instance one's own cache, but instance two's private cache never heard about the change.

Step 4 — Instance two reads Priya's balance again, hits its own private cache, and returns the old value, which is now stale and wrong. This is the drift problem: private per-process caches disagree after a write on one instance.

Step 5 — The same two instances are then wired to a single shared distributed cache. Instance one reads and then write-throughs a new value into the shared cache, and when instance two reads, it hits the same shared cache and sees the fresh value. The shared cache made all instances consistent, which is exactly why you move from Caffeine to Redis as you scale out.

2026-10-24 17:34:10 [INFO] === Write-Through (consistent, slower writes) ===

sections.s6_takeaway:
The main caching patterns differ in who talks to the database and when. In Cache-Aside, which is the default and most common, the application owns the logic: on a read it checks the cache, and on a miss it loads from the database, populates the cache with a time-to-live, and returns the value. Its strengths are that the application is in full control, the cache only holds data that was actually requested, and it degrades gracefully because if the cache is down the application just falls back to the database. Its costs are that the first read of any key is a cold miss and that I have to handle invalidation myself on writes, usually by deleting the entry.

Read-Through moves the load-on-miss responsibility into the cache, so the application only asks the cache and the cache invokes a configured loader on a miss — Caffeine's loading cache is exactly this, and it is convenient when many call sites read the same data. Write-Through and Write-Behind are about the write path. Write-Through writes the cache and the database synchronously before returning, so reads always see the latest value at the cost of slower writes, and it pairs naturally with Read-Through. Write-Behind writes the cache immediately and flushes to the database asynchronously, which gives very fast, high-throughput writes and can batch repeated updates, but it risks losing writes if the cache fails before the flush, so I use it for counters and metrics, never for money movement where every write must be durable.

Choosing among them is driven by the read-write mix and the consistency and durability needs: read-heavy data that tolerates short staleness gets Cache-Aside with a short time-to-live, data that must always reflect the latest write gets Write-Through, and high-write workloads that tolerate eventual durability get Write-Behind. Real systems often combine them, most commonly Cache-Aside reads with explicit invalidation on writes.

The evolution from Caffeine to Redis is driven by going from one instance to many. Caffeine is an in-process cache that is blazing fast because a lookup is just a method call in the same JVM, and it is perfect for a single instance or for reference data. But once I run multiple instances behind a load balancer, each has its own private Caffeine cache, and they drift: a write that updates or invalidates one instance's cache leaves the others serving stale data because they never heard about it, which is unacceptable for something like a balance. The fix is a distributed cache like Redis that lives outside the processes, so all instances read and write the same shared cache and an invalidation from any instance is immediately visible to all, at the cost of a network hop per access and an extra system to operate.

In my banking work I used Cache-Aside for displayed balances with a short time-to-live, moved to Read-Through plus Write-Through when the load-on-miss logic was duplicated everywhere, and when the account service scaled to multiple instances I moved the shared balances to Redis because the private Caffeine caches were drifting after writes. The nuances I always add are that I often run both — a short-lived Caffeine level-one cache in front of a shared Redis level-two cache so the hottest keys are served at nanosecond speed while Redis keeps instances consistent — that deleting a key on write is usually safer than updating it under concurrency, and that any cache with a time-to-live is eventually consistent by definition, so I cache a displayed balance but I always read the authoritative balance from the database when authorizing a debit.
